title: C3: Rethinking Process Supervision viaConfidence-Guided Credit Correction inMulti-Turn Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: C 3 : Rethinking Process Supervision via Confidence-Guided Credit Correction in Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large language models are increasingly trained as multi-turn agents that interact with external tools. However, outcome-only reinforcement learning can produce a form of misguided reinforcement : even on successful trajectories, undesirable local behaviors may receive positive token-level advantages and be favored by the policy update.
To address this issue, we propose Confidence-Guided Credit Correction (C 3 ) , a plug-in method for local credit correction. C 3 identifies spans corresponding to undesirable behaviors and selectively corrects positive credit after advantage estimation, with the correction strength adaptively controlled by the behavior policy’s confidence in the corresponding behavior, while leaving the task reward and original credit estimation unchanged.
Across multiple multi-turn benchmarks, C 3 improves performance under both critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning methods. Injecting the same behavioral signals as turn-level or outcome rewards does not consistently improve performance. Our results show that local credit correction provides an effective form of process supervision for outcome-driven RL.

To address this issue, we propose Confidence-Guided Credit Correction (C 3 ) , a plug-in method for local credit correction. Our results show that local credit correction provides an effective form of process supervision for outcome-driven RL. 1 Introduction Multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for training language agents on complex tasks that require long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool interaction ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Jian et al., 2026 ) . A common approach optimizes agents with outcome-level rewards that evaluate the success of an entire interaction trajectory ( Jin et al., 2025 ) . However, outcome-level supervision provides only sparse and coarse-grained feedback for intermediate behaviors, making it difficult to assign appropriate credit across long-horizon interactions ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . To provide denser supervision for intermediate behaviors, recent work introduces process-level rewards and other process-level signals ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . (a) Mixed credit in undesirable behaviors. (b) Credit construction across optimization paradigms. Figure 1: Misguided reinforcement under outcome-only training. (a) Incorrect tool use and redundant search receive mixed token-level credit, with positive and negative advantages shown in rose and blue-grey . (b) Token-level credit construction in critic-based and critic-free optimization. Our Key Observation. We inspect representative training trajectories under outcome-only training and find that undesirable local behaviors can still receive positive token-level advantages. We identify this phenomenon as a form of misguided reinforcement . More precisely, it is a form of local credit misalignment, where the token-level advantage assigned to an undesirable behavior is inconsistent with its process-level quality. This creates a fundamental mismatch between what behavior should be discouraged and what the policy update favors . Figure 1 (a) shows two representative undesirable behaviors observed. In the invalid tool call, a missing closing tag for <search> causes the call to be malformed, yet the preceding unclosed tokens receive positive advantages while the subsequently closed tokens receive negative advantages. In the redundant search, the same query is issued in consecutive turns, but its tokens also receive mixed advantages. Such misalignment reflects the challenge of assigning localized credit from trajectory-level outcomes. Why Existing Credit Construction Falls Short. Figure 1 (b) illustrates how token-level credit is constructed under two common optimization paradigms. In critic-based reinforcement learning, token-level advantages are estimated through returns and value functions, so a process-level penalty can propagate to tokens beyond the behavior that triggered it. In critic-free methods, relative advantages are derived directly from trajectory-level outcomes, causing local behaviors to inherit credit from the overall trajectory. Thus, the two paradigms differ in how credit is constructed, but share a more fundamental challenge: How can process-level supervision correct a localized undesirable behavior without altering the credit assigned to unrelated behaviors, thereby avoiding credit misalignment? To address this challenge, we propose C 3 (Confidence-Guided Credit Correction) , a lightweight process-level credit correction module that directly operates on token-level advantages. Given undesirable behaviors localized by external process-level supervision, C 3 selectively corrects positive advantages within the corresponding spans, with the correction magnitude adapting to the model’s confidence in the corresponding actions. C 3 introduces no additional process rewards and does not modify the underlying policy optimization objective, making it a plug-in module applicable to both critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning paradigms. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify and characterize misguided reinforcement, where undesirable local behaviors can receive positive policy advantages under outcome-level training, creating a mismatch between behavioral quality and the direction of policy updates. • We propose C 3 , a plug-and-play confidence-guided credit correction framework that rectifies misaligned positive credit within detector-localized undesirable behavior spans without altering task rewards or the underlying RL objective. • We evaluate C 3 across different policy optimization paradigms and multi-turn agent benchmarks. Results show that C 3 reduces positive advantages on detected undesirable-behavior spans, decreases their occurrence, and improves overall agent performance. 2 Related Work Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents. Language agents are commonly optimized with critic-based methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) or group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . They support retrieval ( Jin et al., 2025 ) and long-horizon research or collaboration ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) , but typically learn from trajectory-level outcomes. Consequently, an otherwise successful trajectory may still reinforce undesirable intermediate behaviors. Unlike approaches that modify the overall policy optimization process, C 3 preserves the underlying objective and instead performs localized credit correction on undesirable behavior spans. Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Agents. Credit assignment asks how trajectory-level outcome credit should be attributed to intermediate actions. Hierarchical methods allocate credit across turns ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) , while turn- or step-level estimators align advantages with action boundaries ( Li et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Action-to-token allocation further refines the mapping from outcomes to local advantages ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and retrospective methods estimate each turn’s contribution ( Ekbote et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . C 3 leaves this outcome-to-advantage mapping intact and operates on the resulting token-level advantages. While these approaches refine how outcome credit is distributed, C 3 instead focuses on whether the resulting local credit is consistent with the underlying behavior. Process Supervision for LLM Agents. Process supervision instead asks whether an intermediate behavior is desirable. Process reward models score individual steps ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) ; search agents use step-wise rewards ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , information gain ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , or hindsight signals ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . Judges and self-distillation provide local assessments ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026 ) , while counterfactual attribution derives feedback from alternative rollouts ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . These signals are typically introduced as rewards or advantage shaping. Rather than introducing additional process rewards, C 3 uses localized process feedback to correct positive advantages assigned to undesirable-behavior spans within the existing token-level advantage. 3 Preliminary We consider a multi-turn reinforcement learning setting where an LLM agent interacts with an environment to solve a task. Generally, most positive-advantage tokens correspond to behaviors that are consistent with successful task completion. However, a small subset of tokens may exhibit undesirable behaviors yet receive positive advantages, causing them to be reinforced by the base RL objective. C 3 targets these sparse misassignments by selectively calibrating their advantages, while leaving the remaining tokens, the reward function, and the base advantage estimator unchanged. 4 Methodology We define C 3 as a post-estimation operator for multi-turn agent reinforcement learning. An external transcript detector localizes an undesirable behavior , the base RL pipeline provides token-level advantages, and C 3 corrects these advantages before the actor update. We first motivate this design through an empirical behavioral and credit audit, and then define the inputs, localization rule, and correction operator. Figure 2 summarizes the resulting workflow.
